title: Spermidine reduces peri-implant inflammation and fibrosis to nurture osseointegration

sections.abstract:
Medical implants of exogenous materials often induce foreign body response (FBR) in hosts, which is characterized by inflammation and fibrosis. Herein, composite scaffolds with interpenetrating hard and soft phases were fabricated, consisting of titanium alloy and a biomatrix mimicking extracellular matrix. Spermidine-functionalized biomatrix (CST@GOA) not only inhibits inflammatory response and osteoclastogenesis of macrophages, but also fosters migration and osteogenesis of MC3T3-E1 cells. Interestingly, CST@GOA can mitigate acute inflammation and fibrosis, characteristics of FBR, against silicone implanted in rats. Moreover, bone repair experiments in rabbits show that CST@GOA-interpenetrated porous titanium alloy scaffolds attenuate FBR against metal implants and promote osseointegration. Meanwhile, diethylenetriamine, a polyamine resembling spermidine in chemistry, has been used in place of spermidine to enable ‘operando’ comparison in both cell and animal experiments. Proteomic analysis of rabbit bone tissues reveals that spermidine modulates PI3K-Akt pathway by upregulating PTEN, which may play a pivotal role in coordinating downstream signaling of inflammation, autophagy and bone homeostasis. Together, it is demonstrated that spermidine can endow either synthetic polymers or metal implants with anti -FBR activity by regulating host response and nurture peri-implant niche to improve osseointegration of metal implants. Hence, spermidine affords a natural and elegant strategy to alleviate FBR against medical implants.

Keywords: Medical implants, Foreign body response (FBR), Inflammation, Fibrosis, Spermidine
sections.introduction:
Medical implants made of exogenous materials often induce foreign body response (FBR) of the host immune system [ 1 ], which is characterized by peri-implant inflammation [ 2 ] and possible fibrosis [ 3 , 4 ], when the implant contains non-biodegradable materials. Implants for soft tissue are usually based on biodegradable or non-biodegradable polymers with proper elasticity and tenacity [ 5 , 6 ]. The inflammation caused by biodegradable polymers will be resolved after the degradation of implants [ 7 , 8 ], whereas the unresolved chronic inflammation due to non-biodegradable polymers, such as silicone, may lead to peri-implant fibrosis [ [9] , [10] , [11] ]. Similarly, non-biodegradable metal-based implants, typically used for bone repair, also suffer aseptic inflammation [ 12 ] and fibrous encapsulation, which may impair osseointegration and eventually result in implant failure [ [13] , [14] , [15] , [16] , [17] ]. One common approach to improve the osseointegration of metal implants is to modify implant surface with bioactive coatings containing immunosuppressants such as dexamethasone [ [18] , [19] , [20] , [21] ]. Other strategies often involve the injection of cytokines or neutralizing antibodies [ 19 ]. Unfortunately, these approaches either cause undesirable side effects or incur high cost or suffer inconvenience in administration.

For mammals, male sperm have to enter a female body to complete fertilization, a critical step in natural selection. Unfortunately, female tissues initiate an inflammatory response upon the contact with male seminal fluid [ [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] ]. Indeed, sperm are treated as invaders and attacked by the female immune system in a manner similar to FBR. Yet, mother Nature is so canny that she has made a counter plan to protect sperm, which is carried out by two special agents, spermidine (SPD) and spermine (SPM) [ [26] , [27] , [28] , [29] , [30] ].

Both SPD and SPM are ‘old’ polyamines originally identified in semen [ 31 ]. To date, ample literature has demonstrated that SPD and SPM possess various important cellular functions including immune modulation, autophagy induction, etc . [ [32] , [33] , [34] , [35] ]. However, we are more interested in SPD than SPM for a particular reason. It has been shown that the serum concentration of SPD is roughly 20-fold higher than that of SPM in mice and more importantly, it is the serum concentration of SPD but not that of SPM that significantly declines in older mice [ 36 ]. Although the causality between aging and decreased SPD level in serum is not clear, it is known that the supplementation of SPD can promote longevity [ 37 ]. It is also known that aging is accompanied by systemic chronic inflammation [ [38] , [39] , [40] ]. Hence, we speculate that SPD plays a critical anti-inflammatory role and envision that the local application of SPD in medical implants may down-regulate FBR in hosts, like it does in protecting sperm.

Herein, we show that an SPD-empowered biomatrix (CST@GOA) mimicking extracellular matrix inhibits M1 polarization of macrophages and differentiation of osteoclasts ( Fig. 1 ). More importantly, two non-biodegradable implants, one of silicone and the other based on titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V), demonstrate significantly reduced peri-implant inflammation and fibrosis after modification with CST@GOA. The attenuated host immune response by such a modification on metal implants can be translated into enhanced osseointegration, suggesting that SPD may afford a more natural and likely safer strategy to mitigate FBR against metal implants.

sections.methods:
Gelatin (Gel), spermidine (SPD), diethylenetriamine (DETA), lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from Escherichia coli O55:B5, ascorbic acid, disodium β-glycerophosphate and dexamethasone were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (USA). Sodium alginate (SA), terephthaladehyde (TA), calcium chloride and alkaline hexadecylpyridinium chloride were purchased from Aladdin (China). O -carboxymethyl chitosan (OCMCS) was procured from Yuanye (China). Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane, PDMS, Sylgard 184) was purchased from Dow Corning (USA).

Advanced minimum essential medium (α-MEM), Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM), fetal bovine serum (FBS) and penicillin-streptomycin (P-S) were purchased from Gibco/ThermoFisher Scientific (USA). Recombinant murine sRANK ligand (Receptor Activator of Nuclear Factor-κ B Ligand, RANKL) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent cytokine assay (ELISA) kits for tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), interleukin 4 (IL-4), interleukin 6 (IL-6) and interleukin 10 (IL-10) were purchased from Peprotech (USA).

Live/Dead assay kit and cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) were purchased from Dojindo (Japan). Pluripotent stem cell BCIP/NBT alkaline phosphatase color development kit and alizarin red S (ARS) staining kit were purchased from Beyotime (China). Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) staining kit was purchased from PH Biotechnology (China). Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity assay kit and BCA protein assay kit were purchased from Elabscience (China).

ST and DT crosslinkers were prepared by simply mixing SPD or DETA with TA at the molar ratio of 1.0:1.2 in ethanol at room temperature. For example, to make ST crosslinker of 10 mM, 7.85 μL of SPD (l) and 8 mg of TA (s) were mixed in 5 mL ethanol.

Gel, OCMCS and SA were dissolved in saline at 50 °C to obtain the solution of precursors (GOA). Then the solution of ST or DT was added to obtain single network (SN) biomatrices. The resultant SN biomatrices (ST@GOA and DT@GOA) were immersed in 5 % calcium chloride solution at 4 °C for 1 min to obtain double network (DN) biomatrices (CST@GOA and CDT@GOA). C@GOA matrix was obtained by immersing GOA in 5 % calcium chloride solution following the same procedure.

To prepare biomatrix-interpenetrated scaffold, cylindrical titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) scaffolds (φ = 5.5 mm, h = 5 mm) with triply periodic minimal surfaces (TPMS) were constructed by 3D printing at Nanjing Chamlion (China). The 3D-pinted scaffolds were first dipped in respective SN matrices without Ca 2+ crosslinking, which were pre-warmed at 40 °C to transform into solutions. The scaffolds were quickly centrifuged (20000 rpm) to remove the bubbles and then cooled in a fridge at 4 °C to allow the formation of hydrogel in the pores of the scaffolds as well as on the surface of the scaffolds. Subsequently, the hydrogels on the cooled scaffolds were removed and the porous scaffolds with hydrogels in pores were immersed in 5 wt% calcium chloride solution at 4 °C for 1 min to obtain the porous scaffolds with Ca 2+ -crosslinked biomatrices.

KBr pellets containing samples were characterized by Shimadzu RF-5301PC Fourier transform infrared spectrometer (FT-IR). Solution of crosslinkers were painted on KBr pellets. Powders of freeze-dried matrices were added in KBr pellets. The micro-structure of the biomatrices were observed by Zeiss Gemini Sigma 300 VP scanning electron microscope (SEM). Pore size was analyzed by ImageJ software.

The compression moduli of matrices were measured with an electronic universal testing system (Instron 1121, USA). Specimens were prepared as cylinders (φ = 16 mm, h = 5.5 mm). The compression rate and relaxing rate were both set at 1 mm/min. The compression modulus was estimated from the slope of the linear region (0–10 % strain) of the stress-strain curve by linear fitting.

The rheological properties of SN biomatrices were measured by the Anton Paar MCR 92 rheometer with a 40-mm cone plate. Viscosity measurements were performed at a constant shear rate of 40 s −1 with a heating rate of 2 °C/min, while moduli were measured at a constant strain of 2 % with the same heating rate of 2 °C/min.

Cylindrical matrices (φ = 15 mm, h = 5 mm) were prepared and immersed in oversupplied saline at 37 °C. The weights of swollen matrices at specified time points were recorded as W t1 . The weights of corresponding freeze-dried matrices were recorded as W t2 . The swelling ratio was calculated by equation (1) :

The thermal stabilities of matrices were tested with a TGA 550 thermogravimetric analyzer up to 600 °C, at a heating rate of 10 °C/min.

For in vitro biodegradability, cylindrical samples (φ = 15 mm, h = 5 mm) were first weighted to record the initial weight (W i ) and then immersed in saline (5 mL) containing type I collagenase (5 μg/mL) at 37 °C for 21 days. Samples were weighted at specified time points after brief washing to obtain W t . The weight loss rate was calculated by equation (2) :

The mixture was then centrifuged at 2000 rpm for 10 min. The absorbance of the supernatant was measured at 540 nm with a microplate reader (MOLECULAR DEVICES, SpectraMax Absorbance Reader, CMax Plus, BK-L96C). MC3T3-E1 pre-osteoblasts and RAW 264.7 macrophages were purchased from Procell Life Science & Technology (Wuhan, China). MC3T3-E1 cells were cultured in α-MEM supplemented with 10 % FBS and 1 % P–S at 37 °C under 5 % CO 2 . RAW 264.7 macrophages were maintained in DMEM supplemented with 10 % FBS and 1 % P–S at 37 °C under 5 % CO 2 .

MC3T3-E1 or RAW 264.7 cells were seeded in the lower chambers of 24-well transwell plates (Corning, USA). Free SPD or 150 μL matrices were added to the upper chambers of the transwell plates with 0.4-μm filters. Cell viability was quantified with the CCK-8 kit on Day 1 to Day 7, following the manufacturer's protocol. OD values at 450 nm were recorded with a microplate reader (MOLECULAR DEVICES, SpectraMax Absorbance Reader, CMax Plus, BK-L96C). Cell proliferation was assessed by the live/dead staining assay kit on Day 1 to Day 7 following the manufacturer's protocol. Cells were observed with a fluorescence microscope (Olympus IX53, Japan) and quantified by ImageJ software.

To establish in vitro inflammation model, RAW 264.7 macrophages were seeded in the lower chambers of 24-well transwell plates and then stimulated with 1 μg/mL LPS. 150 μL matrices were added to the upper chambers with 0.4-μm filters. After 24-h treatment, cell morphology was observed with a fluorescence microscope (Olympus IX53, Japan). The supernatants were used in ELISA for TNF-α and IL-6. Cells were lysed for real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) and Western blotting.

To establish in vitro osteoclast differentiation model, RAW 264.7 macrophages were seeded in the lower chambers of 24-well transwell plates and incubated in high-glucose DMEM with 10 % FBS for 24 h. Then the medium was replaced with α-MEM supplemented with 10 % FBS and 100 ng/mL RANKL. 150 μL matrices were added to the upper chambers with 0.4-μm filters. On Day 7, differentiated osteoclasts were stained with TRAP staining kit, following the manufacturer's protocol. Positively stained area was quantified by ImageJ software. Alternatively, cells were also lysed for RT-qPCR and Western blotting.

ELISA for TNF-α, IL-4, IL-6 and IL-10 were performed according to the manufacturer's protocol. For cell culture, 100 μL culture medium was used after proper dilution. For animal tissues, samples were first weighted and added to a homogenization buffer. The mixtures were mechanically homogenized in an ice-water bath to prepare about 10 % (w/v) suspensions. The suspensions were centrifuged at 2500 rpm at 4 °C for 10 min to collect the supernatants. 100 μL supernatant was used after proper dilution.

MC3T3-E1 cells were seeded in the lower chambers of 6-well transwell plates (Corning, USA). Confluent monolayer cells were scratched with sterile 200 μL pipette tips. 150 μL matrices were added to the upper chambers with 0.4-μm filters. The migration of MC3T3-E1 cells was assessed by migration-mediated scratch repair in serum-free medium. Cell images were captured by a microscope (IX53, Olympus, Japan) at designated time points.

The supernatants in the aforementioned osteoclast differentiation culture were collected and mixed with fresh complete α-MEM medium at 1:1 ratio to obtain the osteoclast-inducing medium (OCIM). MC3T3-E1 cells were seeded in the lower chambers of 6-well transwell plates. After 24 h, the seeding medium was replaced with OCIM containing osteogenic factors (50 μg/mL ascorbic acid, 10 mM disodium β-glycerophosphate and 10 nM dexamethasone). 150 μL matrices were added to the upper chambers with 0.4-μm filters. On Days 7 and 14, cells were fixed with 4 % paraformaldehyde for 30 min and stained with the pluripotent stem cell BCIP/NBT alkaline phosphatase color development kit. Alternatively, cells were lysed and total protein levels in cell lysates were determined by the BCA protein assay kit. ALP activity was measured by the alkaline phosphatase activity assay kit and normalized to the total protein level. ARS staining was performed on Days 14 and 21 after fixation with 4 % paraformaldehyde with the ARS staining kit. Images of red calcium nodules were captured by a microscope and a digital camera. Subsequently, ARS-stained cells were incubated with alkaline hexadecylpyridinium chloride and the dissolved ARS was quantified by OD values at 562 nm on a microplate reader.

mRNA levels of interested genes were quantified by RT-qPCR. The sequences of RT-qPCR primers are listed in Tables S1 and S2 . For RAW 264.7 and MC3T3-E1, cells were washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Then, total RNA was extracted with TRIZOL reagent (10296028, Invitrogen, USA) and quantified with a microvolume spectrophotometer (NanoDrop2000, ThermoFisher, USA). For animal tissues, samples were frozen on dry ice and ground for RNA extraction following similar protocols. The extracted RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA with SuperScript 255 III reverse transcription kit (11752050, Invitrogen, USA). RT-qPCR was performed using qPCR SYBR Mix (4472920, Invitrogen, USA) on StepOne software (Applied Biosystems, USA). mRNA levels were normalized to that of β-actin or glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH).

Cells or animal tissues were lysed with RIPA 263 lysis buffer (G2002, Servicebio, China) for 30 min on ice, followed by centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C. The supernatants were collected and the total protein concentrations were determined by BCA protein assay kit (MDL91201, Medical Discovery Leader, China). Lysates were electrophoresed in 10 % SDS-PAGE ( MD911919 , Medical Discovery Leader, China) and then transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes (ISEQ00010, Millipore, USA). After blocking with 5 % nonfat milk in TBST buffer (tris-buffered saline with 0.1 % Tween-20) for 1 h at room temperature, PVDF membranes were incubated with primary antibodies ( Table S3 ) overnight at 4 °C. After washing with TBST for three times, the membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG antibody (1:1000 in TBST) for 1 h at room temperature except for NFATC1 blotting, where HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG antibody (1:2000 in TBST) was used. Subsequently, the blots were washed with TBST for three times and visualized with an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL)-chemiluminescent kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The images were captured with a chemiluminescence imaging system (ChemiScope 6000, CLINX, China). Grayscale intensity levels were quantified with ImageJ software and normalized to respective reference proteins.

All rats were maintained and handled in accordance with the protocol approved by the Committee of Experimental Animal Administration of Jilin GENET-MED Biotechnology Company (approval number: IACUC-2023-020). Original approval documents in Chinese are available from the authors. Before surgery, male SD rats (200–220 g, 8 weeks) were anesthetized by intraperitoneal injection of 2 % tribromoethanol (10 mL/kg). The backs of the rats were shaved and sterilized with iodophor (Mint, China). Four straight incisions about 10 mm were cut with surgical scissors on the back of the same rat. Cylindrical samples (φ = 10 mm, h = 3 mm) were implanted and then the wounds were sutured.

To assess acute FBR, four wounds were made on the back of one rat, with one serving as the sham control and the other three were implanted with three kinds of matrices (C@GOA, CS 500 T@GOA or CD 500 T@GOA). No grouping of rats was done, since each rat was subjected to sham, C@GOA, CS 500 T@GOA and CD 500 T@GOA. Three rats (n = 3x3 = 9) were sacrificed on each of postsurgical Days 3, 7 and 14 (n = 3 each day).

To evaluate chronic FBR caused by biomatrices, four matrices (C@GOA, CS 250 T@GOA, CS 500 T@GOA or CD 500 T@GOA) were implanted into one rat. No grouping of rats was done, since each rat was subjected to C@GOA, CS 250 T@GOA, CS 500 T@GOA or CD 500 T@GOA. Six rats (n = 3 × 2 = 6) were sacrificed on each of postsurgical Day 56 (Week 8) and Day 84 (Week 12) (n = 3 each day).

To evaluate chronic FBR caused by silicone, cylindrical silicone/PDMS discs were made by following the manufacturer's protocol and then modified with matrices (CS 250 T@GOA, CS 500 T@GOA or CD 500 T@GOA) on one side. Silicone only disc and three composite discs (Silicone with C 250 @GOA, Silicone with CS 500 T@GOA or Silicone with CD 500 T@GOA) were implanted into one rat. No grouping of rats was done, since each rat was subjected to Silicone alone, Silicone with C 250 @GOA, Silicone with CS 500 T@GOA or Silicone with CD 500 T@GOA. Six rats (n = 3 × 2 = 6) were sacrificed on each of postsurgical Day 56 (Week 8) and Day 84 (Week 12) (n = 3 each day).

At the specified time points, the remaining matrices and surrounding tissues in the sacrificed animals were photographed. The tissues around the implantation sites were dissected and fixed in 4 % paraformaldehyde or frozen in liquid nitrogen for subsequent analyses.

Fixed tissues from subcutaneous implantation in rats were embedded in paraffin and sliced. The slides were blocked with 5 % bovine serum albumin (BSA) in PBS for 30 min at room temperature and then incubated with primary antibodies ( Table S4 ) overnight at 4 °C. After washing with PBST, samples were incubated with HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG antibody for 50 min at room temperature. After brief washing with PBST, diaminobenzidine (DAB, AiFang, China) was added for color development. Finally, the nuclei were counterstained with hematoxylin (AiFang, China) for 3 min. IHC images were collected by a microscope (E100, Nikon, Japan) and analyzed by ImageJ software.

All rabbits were maintained and handled in accordance with the protocol approved by the Committee of Experimental Animal Administration of Jilin GENET-MED Biotechnology Company (approval number: IACUC-2024-011). Original approval documents in Chinese are available from the authors. New Zealand white rabbits (2.5–3.0 kg, 3 months, n = 30) were anesthetized by intramuscular injection of SU-MIAN-XIN (0.2 mL/kg). Lateral parapatellar incisions were made in rabbit hindlegs. The lateral condyles of the femurs were drilled with a bone drill (φ = 5.5 mm) to create cylindrical defects. Then cylindrical scaffolds (φ = 5.5 mm, h = 5 mm) with or without interpenetrating matrices were implanted in defects, followed by suturing. Rabbits were randomly grouped and subjected to the implantation of the same scaffold. 4 groups of Scaffold alone (Scaffold), Scaffold w/C@GOA, Scaffold w/CS 500 T@GOA and Scaffold w/CD 500 T@GOA (n = 3 each) were euthanized on postsurgical Day 14, whereas 3 groups of Scaffold w/C@GOA, Scaffold w/CS 500 T@GOA and Scaffold w/CD 500 T@GOA (n = 3 each) were sacrificed on postsurgical Day 84. The peri-implants femur tissues were dissected and immersed in 4 % paraformaldehyde or frozen in liquid nitrogen for subsequent analyses.

Fixed tissues from subcutaneous implantation in rats and femur defect repair in rabbits were embedded in paraffin and sliced. Before embedding, rabbit femur tissues were also trimmed, decalcified by 10 % ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid and dehydrated. The sections were subjected to Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) and Masson's trichrome (M-T) stainings as previously described. TRAP staining was performed according the manufacturer's protocol. The images were collected by a microscope (E100, Nikon, Japan) and analyzed by ImageJ software.

Fixed rabbit femur tissues were scanned by desktop micro-CT scanner (μCT 45, Scanco). 151 continuous layers were used to reconstruct the model of bone and implants by NRecon software. Key structure parameters of bones, i.e. , bone mineral density (BMD), bone volume fraction (bone volume/total volume, BV/TV), bone surface density (bone surface/total volume, BS/TV), trabeculae number (Tb.N.), trabecular spacing (Tb.Sp.), trabecular thickness (Tb.Th.) and trabecular pattern factor (Tb.Pf.) were estimated by CTan software.

Rabbit femur samples decalcified by 10 wt% ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid were embedded in paraffin and sliced. The slides were blocked with 5 % BSA in PBS for 30 min at room temperature and then incubated with primary antibodies ( Table S5 ) overnight at 4 °C. After washing with PBST, samples were incubated with HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG antibody for 50 min at room temperature, briefly washed and then incubated with Cy3-tyramine (1:500, G1223, Servicebio, Wuhan, China) for 20 min at room temperature.

For double IF, the samples stained with the first primary antibody were washed with PBST under microwave (high power for 8 min, resting for 8 min and mid-low power for 7 min). After re-blocking with 5 % BSA for 10 min, the slides were incubated with another primary antibody at 4 °C overnight. After washing with PBST, the slides were incubated with HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG antibody for 50 min at room temperature, briefly washed and then incubated with iF488-tyramine (1:500, G1231, Servicebio, Wuhan, China) for 20 min at room temperature.

The nuclei were counterstained by 2-(4-amidinophenyl)-6-indolecarbamidine dihydrochloride (DAPI, 5 μg/mL) for 10 min at room temperature. IF images were collected by a fluorescence microscope (Eclipse C1, Nikon, Japan). All images were analyzed by ImageJ software. The antibodies used in IF were listed in Table S5 .

For quantitative proteomic analysis, 4D-data-independent acquisition (DIA) was performed on the bone tissues around Ti-6Al-4V scaffold (Scaffold), Scaffold with C@GOA (C@GOA), Scaffold with CS 500 T@GOA (CST@GOA) and Scaffold with CD 500 T@GOA (CDT@GOA). PTM BIO company (Hangzhou, China) provided technical support, testing and data acquisition.

The samples were grinded within liquid nitrogen and treated with lysis buffer. Then the supernatants were collected by centrifugation at 12,000 g at 4 °C, followed by protein concentration measurement with BCA protein assay kit. The samples were then mixed with pre-cooled acetone by vertexing and incubated at −20 °C for 2 h. The precipitated proteins were washed 3 times with pre-cooled acetone and re-dissolved in triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB). Trypsin was added to the samples at a 1:50 trypsin-to-protein mass ratio for overnight digestion. The samples were then reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol for 30 min at 56 °C. Subsequently alkylation was carried out with 11 mM iodoacetamide for 15 min at room temperature in the dark. Finally, the peptides were purified with a Strata X solid-phase extraction (SPE) column.

For LC–MS/MS analysis, the tryptic peptides were dissolved and directly loaded onto a reversed phase analytical column. Peptides were separated by gradient elution at a constant flow rate of 500 nL/min on a NanoElute UHPLC system (Bruker Daltonics). The peptides were subjected to capillary ionization followed by the timsTOF Pro mass spectrometry. The electrospray voltage applied was 1.75 kV. Precursors and fragments were analyzed by the TOF detector. The timsTOF Pro was operated in data independent parallel accumulation serial fragmentation (dia-PASEF) mode. The full MS scan was set as 300–1500 ( m/z scan range) and 20 PASEF (MS/MS mode) scans were acquired per cycle. The MS/MS scan range was set as 400–850 and isolation window was set as 7 m/z .

The DIA data were processed by using DIA-NN search engine (v.1.8). Tandem mass spectra were searched against Oryctolagus_cuniculus_9986_PR_20240704.fasta (41458 entries) concatenated with reverse decoy database. Trypsin/P was specified as cleavage enzyme allowing up to 1 missing cleavage. Excision on N-terminal Met and carbamidomethyl on Cys were specified as fixed modification. False discovery rate was adjusted to <1 %.

For Gene Ontology (GO) analysis, GO IDs of the identified proteins were extracted by the EggNOG-mapper software based on the EggNOG database (v5.0.2, http://eggnog5.embl.de/#/app/home ). Then classification and functional annotation were performed on the proteins according to cellular components, molecular functions, and biological processes. Protein pathways were annotated based on the KEGG pathway database, including KAAS (2015, http://www.genome.jp/kegg/kaas/ ), KEGG mapper (v5.0, http://www.kegg.jp/kegg/mapper.html ), and KOBAS (v3.0, http://kobas.cbi.pku.edu.cn/ ). Proteins were identified by BLAST (blastp, evalue ≤ 1e-4) for each sequence and the annotation was based on the top-scoring hit result. PTM BIO company (Hangzhou, China) provided bioinformatic methods and analysis.

All data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (S.D.). The Shapiro‒Wilk normality test was conducted to verify the normal distribution of the data. For pairwise comparisons between two groups, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test was used. For comparisons among three or more groups, one-way ANOVA was performed, followed by Tukey's multiple comparison test to analyze all pairwise differences among groups. GraphPad Prism (v.9.5.1) and OriginPro (2024b) were used for statistical analyses. Statistical significance is denoted as ∗: p < 0.05, ∗∗: p < 0.01, and ∗∗∗: p < 0.001.
sections.results:
The SPD-functionalized biomatrix CST@GOA was prepared in three steps as illustrated in Fig. 2 A. First, g elatin (Gel), O -carboxymethyl chitosan (OCMCS), and sodium a lginate (SA) were mixed to form a temperature-sensitive hydrogel (GOA) based on electrostatic interaction and hydrogen bonds. Gel (G) can provide the cell-adhesive RGD motif and enhance biocompatibility [ 41 ]. OCMCS (O) can afford amino groups to form dynamic imine bonds. Alginate (A) can enhance the stability of the biomatrix after the cross-linking with calcium ion. Second, an ST crosslinker consisting of s permidine and t erephthalaldehyde (TA) was introduced to yield an injectable biomatrix (ST@GOA) with dynamic imine bonds. Third, ST@GOA hydrogel was immersed in CaCl 2 solution to obtain c alcium-chelated CST@GOA biomatrix. Alternatively, ST@GOA could be infused into a scaffold and then crosslinked with Ca 2+ to achieve a composite with interpenetrating soft and hard phases. In this work, we ignored the contribution from the weak electrostatic interaction and hydrogen bonds and thus considered the ST@GOA hydrogel with covalently crosslinked network as single network (SN) biomatrix. Consequently, the CST@GOA with both covalent crosslinking and Ca 2+ chelation networks was named as double network (DN) biomatrix. The formation of imine bonds in ST crosslinker and ST@GOA biomatrix were verified by FT-IR ( Fig. S1 ).

Synthesis and in vitro characterization of SPD-functionalized Biomatrix. (A) Schematic illustration for the preparation of CST@GOA (with or without scaffold) and crosslinking mechanisms. (B) Images of MC3T3-E1 cocultured with various biomatrices in transwells on Days 1 and 3 (n = 3). (C) Chemical structures of SPD and DETA. (D) Cell viabilities of RAW 264.7 and MC3T3-E1 cocultured with various biomatrices in transwells (n = 6). (E) Hemolytic rates for various biomatrices (n = 3). (∗: P < 0.05; ∗∗: P < 0.01; ∗∗∗: p < 0.001; N.S.: not significant).

An optimal ratio of Gel:OCMCS:SA in ST@GOA biomatrix was determined by rheological tests. Previously, we have reported an injectable hydrogel with Gel:OCMCS at 4:1 (6.0 wt%:1.5 wt%) to roughly mimic the composition of extracellular matrix (ECM) [ [42] , [43] , [44] , [45] ]. In this work, we kept the ratio of Gel:OCMCS at 4:1 and substituted a portion of OCMCS with SA for the sake of Ca 2+ crosslinking. Three ratios of Gel:OCMCS:SA including 6:1:0.5, 6:0.75:0.75 and 6:0.5:1 were tested, which were named as GO H A, GO E A E and GOA H respectively ( Table S6 ). The viscosity of ST@GOA increases as the SA concentration increases and the OCMCS content decreases ( Fig. S2 ). The comparison between GO H A and S 100 T@GO H A also indicates that the introduction of ST crosslinker can significantly enhance the viscosity of the GOA hydrogel. The subscript number in S 100 T@GO H A denotes the final micromolar (μM) concentration of SPD loaded in biomatrices and same notation rule is applied afterwards.

The SEM images of Ca 2+ -crosslinked GO H A, GO E A E , GOA H and S 100 T@GO H A hydrogels (named as C@GO H A, C@GO E A E , C@GOA H and CS 100 T@GO H A respectively) corroborate with the findings of rheological tests. The pore size decreases as the concentration of SA rises, whereas the additional crosslinking by ST crosslinker renders even smaller micropores ( Fig. S3 ). The mechanical strength of Ca 2+ -crosslinked GOA hydrogels also elevates as the content of SA increases, which can be further boosted by the ST crosslinker ( Fig. S4 ). In line with the findings of pore size, the increase of SA content in Ca 2+ -crosslinked hydrogels can also lead to smaller swelling ratio and less degradability ( Figs. S5 and S6A ). Notably, Ca 2+ -crosslinked hydrogels (C@GO H A, C@GO E A E , and C@GOA H ) retained well-defined shapes after immersion in saline with type I collagenase for 21 days ( Fig. S6B ), demonstrating good stabilities in vitro . Unlike the findings for pore size and mechanical strength, the formation of dynamic imine network by the ST crosslinker can only slightly change the swelling ratio and degradability, probably due to the dynamic nature of imine bonds in aqueous solution [ 46 ]. It should also be noted that both GOA and ST@GOA are injectable before Ca 2+ -crosslinking ( Fig. S7A ) and will transform into solution at 37 °C ( Fig. S7B ). In contrast, CST@GOA after Ca 2+ -crosslinking can maintain the fixed shape at 37 °C ( Fig. S6B ).

Since a less viscous hydrogel is easier to infuse into porous scaffolds, we chose GO H A (Gel:OCMCS:SA of 6:0.5:1) for subsequent experiments. The storage modulus (G′) and loss modulus (G″) were examined for GO H A and S 100 T@GO H A under different temperatures to determine a proper operation temperature for infusion ( Fig. S8 ). The G's of both GO H A and S 100 T@GO H A are evidently higher than the corresponding G″s under 20 °C, but rapidly decline to be lower than G″s in the rage of 20–40 °C, indicating a transition from a gel state at 20 °C to a solution at 40 °C. GO H A and ST@GO H A display similar sol-gel transition temperatures (T sol/gel ) in the range of 30∼33 °C. Thus, the infusion temperature for ST@GO H A was determined as 45 °C. Hereafter, GO H A with determined composition is renamed as GOA for subsequent characterizations and experiments.

The biocompatibility of DN biomatrices with different concentrations of SPD was evaluated by a coculturing system using transwells. MC3T3-E1 cells exhibit good cell viability when cocultured with biomatrices containing up to 250 μM SPD ( Fig. 2 B and S9A ). Meanwhile, a bioequivalent method was adopted to triangulate the release behavior of SPD from the biomatrices. Notably, free SPD compound causes cytotoxicity on MC3T3-E1 cells at concentrations higher than 2.5 μM ( Fig. S9B ), whereas similar cytotoxicity is only observed for CST@GOA with SPD higher than 500 μM ( Fig. S9A ). So, as a rough estimation, the CS 250 T@GOA and CS 500 T@GOA hydrogels correlate with 1.0 μM and 2.5 μM free SPD at 24 h, respectively. These bioequivalent data suggest that our SPD-functionalized biomatrices sustain a slow release of SPD due to crosslinking by imine bonds. Such a slow release behavior will not cause a high accumulated concentration of SPD in the coculturing system, given that SPD is a natural compound that can be quickly utilized by cells. Although we are unable to demonstrate the exact release profile of SPD at the current stage, we have chosen diethylenetriamine (DETA), a compound structurally similar to SPD but without known biological function, as the control molecule for SPD to ensure that the bioactivities observed for CST@GOA biomatrices are indeed contributed by the function of SPD. SPD and DETA share similar amino groups and charges, with SPD having one additional methylene group on one arm of the secondary amine and two additional methylene groups on the other arm ( Fig. 2 C). Hence, a control crosslinker (DT) of D ETA and T A was synthesized and subsequently used in the preparation of control biomatrices (DT@GOA and CDT@GOA). It is worth mentioning that CDT@GOA and CST@GOA share similar morphology, pore size, mechanical properties and degradation profiles due to the high resemblance between DETA and SPD in chemical structure ( Figs. S3, S4 and S6 ). RAW 264.7 macrophages cocultured with CS 250 T@GOA and CD 250 T@GOA display comparable cell viabilities ( Fig. 2 D). In contrast, MC3T3-E1 cells cocultured with CS 250 T@GOA exhibit better proliferation on Day 7, suggesting a pro-proliferation role of SPD. The hemocompatibility of various biomatrices was assessed by hemolytic rate (HR). The HRs of C@GOA, CS 250 T@GOA and CD 250 T@GOA are less than 2.5 % ( Fig. 2 E), indicating an excellent hemocompatibility below the ASTM standard (F756:2008) of 5% [ 47 ].

Three Ca 2+ -crosslinked GOA matrices (C/CST/CDT@GOA) were implanted subcutaneously in rats to investigate the effects of SPD on FBR in vivo ( Fig. 3 A). Unlike the stagnant cell culture, the circulation in animals may effectively reduce the local concentration of SPD. It should also be noted that SPD is a small molecule that can be metabolized by most of mammalian cells and the concentration of SPD in mammalian semen can be as high as a few mM [ 30 , 48 ]. So, higher concentration of SPD can be tolerated in the in vivo experiments owing to the circulation and much larger number of SPD-consuming cells. Indeed, our previous experiments have shown that higher SPD concentration can be used in animals than in cell culture experiments to achieve better results in immunomodulation [ 44 ]. Hence, although our in vitro experiments find good cell viability for biomatrices containing up to 250 μM SPD ( Fig. 2 B), we wondered whether the doubled loading concentration of SPD would result in better anti -FBR activities in vivo . Hence, both CS 250 T@GOA and CS 500 T@GOA were used in our subcutaneous implantation, together with CD 500 T@GOA which was chosen as the comparison for the higher loading concentration of SPD in the experiments.

The resulting acute FBR was evaluated by the inflammatory response on post-implantation Days 3, 7 and 14. Macroscopically, CS 500 T@GOA shows a more transparent appearance and less peri-implant inflammation, whereas the implants of C@GOA and CD 500 T@GOA are blurry and surrounded by swollen tissues representing inflammatory microenvironments ( Fig. S10 ). Pathologically, H&E staining of peri-implant tissues revealed that CS 500 T@GOA suppressed the infiltration of immune cells to implants when compared with C@GOA and CD 500 T@GOA ( Fig. 3 B), in line with our previous findings [ 44 , 45 ]. Notably, an inflammatory cavity caused by surgery could be observed on Day 3 in the sham operation group and this inflamed site has been transformed to a non-inflammatory one by SPD-containing CS 500 T@GOA. Moreover, RT-qPCR indicated that the mRNA levels of pro-inflammatory interleukin 6 ( Il-6 ) and tumor necrosis factor α ( Tnf-α ) were reduced for CS 500 T@GOA compared to those of C@GOA and CD 500 T@GOA; and the mRNA levels of anti-inflammatory genes, such as interleukin 10 ( Il-10 ) and arginase 1 ( Arg1 ), were increased in peri-implant tissues ( Fig. S11 ). Concordantly, IHC staining exhibited a decreased M1 macrophage marker (T-lymphocyte activation antigen CD86, CD86) and an increased M2 macrophage marker (scavenger receptor cysteine-rich type 1 protein M130, CD163) ( Fig. 3 C and D). Pro-inflammatory mediators, i.e. , IL-6, inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS or NOS2), TNF-α and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), were found to be reduced in peri-CS 500 T@GOA tissues, while the levels of IL-10 were elevated. The downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, IL-6 and TNF-α, and upregulation of anti-inflammatory cytokines, interleukin 4 (IL-4) and IL-10, by CS 500 T@GOA (S) were also confirmed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) of peri-implant tissues in comparison with CD 500 T@GOA (D) and sham operation (Sh) ( Fig. 3 E and S12 ). Previously, we have proposed that SPD-functionalized biomaterials may mitigate implant-induced inflammation via the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) pathway based on published literature [ 45 , [49] , [50] , [51] , [52] , [53] ]. Herein, Western blotting on extracts of the peri-implant tissues confirmed our previous findings. SPD-functionalized biomatrix activates AMPK in surrounding tissues, which inhibits p65 and IκB phosphorylation as well as the phosphorylation of mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) ( Fig. 3 F and G). Hence, our subcutaneous implantation results suggest that SPD can, indeed, reduce the inflammatory response of acute FBR in vivo , which is possibly mediated via the AMPK/NF-κB/mTOR pathway.

Next, we wondered whether SPD could attenuate chronic FBR, which is typically manifested as fibrous encapsulation. H&E and Masson stainings of tissues surrounding remaining Ca 2+ -crosslinked GOA implants on Days 56 and 84 revealed significantly less collagen deposition for CST@GOA, in contrast with those of C@GOA and CD 500 T@GOA ( Fig. 4 A and B). More importantly, such an effect on collagen deposition also depends on SPD concentration, since the amount of per-implant collagen decreases from C@GOA to CS 250 T@GOA and to CS 500 T@GOA ( Fig. 4 B). CS 500 T@GOA reduced long-term collagen deposition as suggested by the comparison of incremental collagen area from post-implantation Day 56 to Day 84 ( Fig. S13 ). Furthermore, no pathological changes were observed in the major organs (including hearts, livers, spleens, lungs and kidneys) of rats implanted with CS 500 T@GOA and CD 500 T@GOA on Days 7 and 84, indicating a good biosafety ( Fig. S14 ).

The composite disc of Silicone-CS 500 T@GOA (SS) also downregulated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6 and TNF-α) and upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-4 and IL-10) on Day 14 ( Fig. 3 E and S12 ). Encouraged by the reduced FBR observed for CST@GOA on synthetic polymer (silicone) in the hypodermis, we envisioned that CST@GOA could also attenuate the FBR caused by metal implants in bones. However, it is difficult to stably modify bulk metal surface with our matrices. Thus, we proposed to infuse porous titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) scaffolds with our matrices to achieve stable and durable biomodification. To this end, we have adopted a porous structure with triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) based on existing literature [ 54 ] and fabricated porous Ti-6Al-4V scaffolds by 3D printing. Then three matrices, C@GOA, CS 500 T@GOA and CD 500 T@GOA, were infused into the interconnected pores of the TPMS scaffolds. The infused composites were immersed in a CaCl 2 solution to obtain hybrid implants of hard metal backbone with interpenetrating soft Ca 2+ -crosslinked GOA matrices ( Fig. 1 and S15 ). The hard-soft composites (TPMS scaffolds with matrices), as well as TPMS scaffolds without hydrogel modification, were implanted into holes drilled in femoral condyles of rabbits to investigate the functionality of SPD-empowered metal implants in vivo ( Fig. S16 ).

The peri-implant tissues on post-implantation Days 42 and 84 were examined to see whether the inhibition of acute FBR by CS 500 T@GOA could translate into better osseointegration. As shown in the reconstructed micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) images, more new bone (yellow) was formed around the scaffold with CS 500 T@GOA (white) than those of the other groups ( Fig. 5 A). Meanwhile, more bone was observed in the pores of CS 500 T@GOA-in terpenetrated scaffold in the reconstructed axial and longitudinal planes. Quantitively, the SPD-empowered scaffolds increased the bone mineral density (BMD), bone volume fraction (bone volume/total volume, BV/TV) and bone surface density (bone surface/total volume, BS/TV) of peri-implant tissues ( Fig. 5 B). Further characterization of trabecular bones demonstrates that the trabeculae number (Tb.N.) and trabecular spacing (Tb.Sp.) are also enlarged in the tissue surrounding the CS 500 T@GOA scaffold ( Fig. 5 B), but no significant change of trabecular thickness (Tb.Th.) was observed ( Fig. S17 ). Notably, the trabecular structure regenerated with the CS 500 T@GOA scaffold exhibits a lower trabecular pattern factor (Tb.Pf.), an indicator for osteoporosis. These findings demonstrate that the SPD-empowered composite scaffold can indeed direct better bone regeneration and osseointegration.

To investigate the effect of SPD on acute FBR against metal implants, immunofluorescence (IF) stainings against CD68, CD86 and CD206 were performed on post-implantation Day 14. It is found CS 500 T@GOA-interpenetrated scaffolds yielded significantly higher CD206 + /CD68 + ratio and lower CD86 + /CD68 + ratio than the TPMS scaffold alone and TPMS scaffolds with C@GOA and CD 500 T@GOA ( Fig. 5 C-E and S18), suggesting mitigated inflammatory responses and accelerated transition from M1 macrophage-dominated phase to M2 macrophage-dominated phase. Corroboratively, H&E staining revealed that the peri-implant tissues surrounding the TPMS scaffold alone and TPMS scaffolds with C@GOA and CD 500 T@GOA were infiltrated by abundant immune cells on post-implantation Day 14 ( Fig. 5 F). Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) staining showed that osteoclasts, the major inflammation-activated effector cells in bones, had been recruited to peri-implant sites (indicated by arrows in Fig. 5 F). In contrast, the tissues around the CS 500 T@GOA-interpenetrated scaffolds exhibited evidently fewer immune cells and osteoclasts, indicating attenuated FBR. Given the importance of angiogenesis in inflammatory response and osseointegration, IF staining against common angiogenesis markers, CD31 and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), was conducted. Significantly higher levels of CD31 and VEGF were found in the tissues surrounding CS 500 T@GOA-interpenetrated scaffolds than the tissues around the TPMS scaffold alone and TPMS scaffolds with C@GOA and CD 500 T@GOA ( Fig. S19 ), suggesting that SPD enhanced the angiogenesis in peri-implant tissues for better osseointegration. Meanwhile, no pathological changes were found in the hearts, livers, spleens, lungs and kidneys of rabbits with implanted scaffolds on Day 14, suggesting an excellent biosafety ( Fig. S20 ).

Furthermore, chronic FBR against the implanted scaffolds was examined by IF staining against actin alpha 2 (ACTA2 or α-SMA) and collagen type III alpha 1 (COL3A1), two known markers for fibrosis in bones [ 15 ], on post-implantation Day 42 and Day 84. As expected, CST@GOA-interpenetrated scaffolds resulted in thinner and less dense fibrous capsules around the implants than TPMS scaffold alone and CDT@GOA-interpenetrated scaffolds ( Fig. S21 ). Together, these results implicate that SPD reduces both the acute and chronic FBR caused by metal implants and nurtures osseointegration.

Crosstalk between osteoblasts and osteoclasts is essential to maintain bone homeostasis, which determines the fate of implants and osseointegration [ 19 , 55 , 56 ]. To verify the biological effects of CST@GOA on osteogenesis in vitro , we prepared an osteoclast-inducing medium (OCIM) by mixing the supernatant of osteoclast culture with fresh α-MEN medium at the ratio of 1:1 and then examined the influence of CST@GOA on the migration and osteogenic differentiation of non-transformed MC3T3-E1 cells in OCIM with osteogenic factors ( Fig. 6 A). The migration of MC3T3-E1 cells was assessed by a scratch healing assay. The MC3T3-E1 cells cocultured with CS 250 T@GOA demonstrated faster migration-mediated scratch repair than the cells cocultured with the other matrices ( Fig. 6 B), indicating an enhanced cell migration. Subsequently, the osteogenesis of MC3T3-E1 was evaluated in OCIM in presence of dexamethasone, ascorbic acid and β-glycerophosphate by alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and alizarin red S (ARS) stainings. The MC3T3-E1 cocultured with CS 250 T@GOA exhibited larger purple area in ALP staining and higher ALP activity than those treated with C@GOA and CD 250 T@GOA on Days 7 and 14 ( Fig. 6 C and D). Consistently, ARS staining revealed a larger brown area and higher mineralization level for MC3T3-E1 cocultured with CS 250 T@GOA on Days 14 and 21 ( Fig. 6 E and F). Elevated expression of osteoblast-related genes, i.e. runt-related transcription factor 2 ( RUNX2 ), osterix ( Osx ), osteopontin ( Spp1 ), osteocalcin ( Bglap ) and ALP ( Alpl ), was also validated at the mRNA level for MC3T3-E1 cocultured with CS 250 T@GOA on Day 3 ( Fig. 6 G). In addition, Western blotting confirmed the upregulated protein levels of RUNX2, OSX, SPP1 and BGLAP by CS 250 T@GOA on Day 7 ( Fig. 6 H and I). Together, these results demonstrate that SPD can promote migration and osteogenesis at cellular level, which agrees with our in vivo observations ( Fig. 5 A and B).

Macrophages play a crucial role in implant-induced inflammation [ 1 , 57 , 58 ] and bone homeostasis [ [59] , [60] , [61] ]. Hence, two cell models were set up to verify the immunomodulatory effects and osteoclastogenesis for various biomatrices ( Fig. 7 A). One is RAW 264.7 macrophages with high-glucose DMEM in presence of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and the other is RAW 264.7 cells with advanced MEM in presence of receptor activator of nuclear factor (NF)-κB ligand (RANKL). Corresponding morphological changes of RAW 264.7 macrophages can also be observed under the microscope ( Fig. 7 D). Cells treated with CS 250 T@GOA displayed markedly fewer podosomes than those with other matrices, suggesting that CS 250 T@GOA transformed M1 macrophages into M2 phenotype, in line with our previous reports [ 44 , 45 ]. The downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines and M1 macrophage markers including Tnf , Il1β , Il6 , nitric oxide synthase 2 ( Nos2 ) and Cd86 was validated at the mRNA level for RAW 264.7 cells treated with CS 250 T@GOA ( Fig. 7 E and S22 ), as well as the upregulated expression of anti-inflammatory genes and M2 macrophage markers, such as Il10 , Arg1 , transforming growth factor β 1 ( Tgfb1 ) and Cd206 . Western blotting was used to further confirm the reduced expression of M1 phenotype marker, iNOS (NOS2), and the increased levels of the M2 phenotype marker, CD206 ( Fig. 7 F).

Our in vivo results suggest that SPD reduces the inflammatory response of acute FBR via the AMPK/NF-κB/mTOR pathway ( Fig. 3 F). Here, we find that SPD can indeed enhance the phosphorylation of AMPK and suppress the phosphorylation of IκBα and p65 in LPS-stimulated macrophages ( Fig. 7 F). Such a regulation in AMPK/NF-κB signaling not only explains the anti-inflammatory role of SPD observed in vivo , but also implies that CS 250 T@GOA has the potential to inhibit osteoclastogenesis and induce autophagy, since AMPK/NF-κB pathway has been implicated in osteoclastogenesis and autophagy [ [62] , [63] , [64] , [65] ]. Hence, we investigated the effect of CST@GOA on the osteoclastogenesis of RAW 264.7 cells in presence of RANKL ( Fig. 7 G and H). RAW 264.7 cells treated with CST@GOA resulted in fewer differentiated osteoclasts than those observed with the other matrices. Corroboratively, the reduced transcription of osteoclast-related genes, cathepsin K ( CtsK ), tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase 5 ( Trap5b ) and matrix metalloprotease 9 ( Mmp9 ) is also found ( Fig. 7 I), which is in line with the downregulated expression of nuclear factor of activated T cells 1 (NFATc1) observed in CST@GOA-treated cells ( Fig. 7 J). Meanwhile, the inhibition of mTOR phosphorylation by AMPK activation is observed ( Fig. 7 F), suggesting that CST@GOA may enhance autophagy in macrophages. To this end, the downstream effectors of autophagy were examined. The altered ratio of LC3β I to LC3β II and downregulation of p62 were verified in both LPS- and RANKL-induced macrophages ( Fig. 7 J). Our in vitro data corroborates with the in vivo finding that CST@GOA inhibits FBR-induced inflammation and osteoclast differentiation ( Fig. 3 , Fig. 5 ). Although, we are unable to elucidate a clear mechanism of how SPD orchestrates the complex signaling resulting in cytokine production, autophagy and osteoclast differentiation at this stage, we have highlighted some SPD-regulated targets ( Fig. 7 K), which will be further examined with our proteomic data.

To further investigate the mechanism of SPD-functionalized biomatrix in osseointegration, quantitative proteomics was used to measure protein expression in the peri-implant bone tissues surrounding C@GOA, CST@GOA, or CDT@GOA-interpenetrated scaffolds as well as the TPMS scaffolds without matrices (Scaffold). A total of 40424 peptides and 6533 proteins were identified. Principal component analysis (PCA) reveals significant differences among these groups and particularly, the CST@GOA group exhibits a proteomic profile distinct from the others ( Fig. 8 A). Interestingly, CST@GOA and CDT@GOA groups are located in the opposite directions from C@GOA on PC1 axis, implying that SPD and DETA yield contrary effects when used in biomaterials. A comparison between CST@GOA and CDT@GOA shows 268 downregulated proteins and 253 upregulated proteins (fold change >1.5, p < 0.05) ( Fig. 8 B and S23 ). Fewer differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) are hit in CST@GOA vs. C@GOA (148 upregulated and 273 downregulated proteins) and CDT@GOA vs. C@GOA (131 upregulated and 74 downregulated proteins). The larger number of DEPs (521 in total) observed in CST@GOA vs. CDT@GOA suggests that although SPD and DETA only display a minor difference in chemical structure, SPD regulates some biological functions that DETA either doesn't alter or alters in the opposite manner, which agrees with the trend seen on the PC1 axis ( Fig. 8 A).

Gene Ontology (GO) analysis demonstrates significant enrichment in acute and chronic inflammatory responses, activation of T-helper, T and B cells, macrophage activation and differentiation, osteoclast differentiation and skeletal system development for CST@GOA vs. CDT@GOA ( Fig. S24 ). In terms of proteins involved in immune responses, CST@GOA vs. Scaffold yields 48/51 up-/down-regulated proteins, while CDT@GOA vs. Scaffold only exhibits 12/18 up-/down-regulated proteins, which suggests that CST@GOA induced a stronger immune response than CDT@GOA did ( Fig. 8 C). As for inflammatory responses, CST@GOA vs. Scaffold yielded 22/35 up-/down-regulated proteins, much higher than those of CDT@GOA vs. Scaffold ( Fig. 8 D). In line with our previous results, it is found that anti-inflammatory ARG1 is upregulated by CST@GOA vs. either CDT@GOA or Scaffold, whereas several pro-inflammatory members of matrix metalloproteases (MMPs) and signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) family are downregulated, including MMP1 [ 66 ], MMP9 [ 67 ], STAT1 [ 68 ], and STAT3 [ 69 ]. Notably, tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 1 (TRAF1) is found to be downregulated by CST@GOA. TRAF1 mediates tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) signaling to NF-κB activation through the receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1) [ [70] , [71] , [72] ]. Indeed, the downregulation of RIPK1, a recently reported target of SPD-mediated acetylhypusination, is also observed in CST@GOA vs. either CDT@GOA or Scaffold, which is consistent with the previous work [ 73 ].

More interestingly, some inflammation-related proteins are found to be oppositely altered by SPD and DETA. Tyrosine kinase binding protein (TYROBP), chitotriosidase-1 (CHIT1), and non-enzymatic chitinase-3 like-protein-1 (CHI3L1 or YKL-40) are up-regulated by C@GOA and CDT@GOA, but downregulated by CST@GOA ( Fig. 8 E). TYROBP expressed in macrophages and osteoclasts is known to amplify intracellular signals to activate NF-κB pathway and trigger pro-inflammatory cytokine production [ [74] , [75] , [76] ]. The upregulation of TYROBP in CDT@GOA vs. C@GOA and the downregulation in CST@GOA vs. C@GOA demonstrate the opposite functions of SPD and DETA in inflammation, where DETA intensifies inflammatory response to exogenous biomaterials ( i.e. gelatin, OCMCS, alginate) but SPD reduces it. CHIT1 and CHI3L1 are two members in 18-glycosyl hydrolase (18-GH) family with high capability to bind with chitin, which are implicated in inflammatory responses with the high expression under various acute and chronic inflammatory conditions [ [77] , [78] , [79] , [80] ]. The upregulation of CHIT1 and CHI3L1 by C@GOA and CDT@GOA are probably due to the presence of chitin-derived OCMCS in GOA. Such an upregulation is reversed by CST@GOA, indicating an effective role of SPD in inhibiting inflammation caused by exogenous biomaterials. Together, these results demonstrate that the subtle molecular difference between SPD and DETA may cause distinct inflammatory outcomes as we previously reported [ 45 ].

It should also be noted that the aforementioned inflammation-related proteins ( e.g. STAT1/3, MMP1/9, RIPK1, TYROBP, CHIT1, CHI3L1) are repeatedly found downregulated in the DEPs for the productions of IL-1, IL-6, IL-10 and TNF-α ( Fig. S25 ), which is consistent with our observations in rat subcutaneous implantation ( Fig. 3 C-E), rabbit femoral condyle repair ( Fig. 5 C-E) and cell culture ( Fig. 7 B, C and 7E).

As for bone homeostasis, only 5 upregulated proteins were identified for CST@GOA vs. CDT@GOA, but 24 proteins were downregulated ( Fig. 8 F). Several proteins involved in both the inflammatory response and osteoclast proliferation and differentiation were again seen to be downregulated, including MMP9 [ 81 ], STAT3 [ 82 ], CHIT1, CHI3L1 [ 83 , 84 ] and TYROBP [ 85 , 86 ] ( Fig. S26 ). Hence, it is believed that the bone-regenerating function of CST@GOA is mainly mediated by inhibiting osteoclast activation. It is noteworthy that the reduced expression of MMP9 by CST@GOA in vivo agrees with our in vitro results ( Fig. 7 I), and the downregulation of STAT3 might explain the decreased level of NFATc1 observed in vitro ( Fig. 7 J). Interestingly, TGF-β1 and mothers against decapentaplegic homolog 2 (SMAD2) were upregulated by CST@GOA ( Fig. 8 F). TGF-β1 is known to promote the proliferation and chemotaxis of osteoprogenitor cells via SMAD-dependent pathway [ 87 , 88 ], while inhibiting osteoclast differentiation. Thus, the upregulation of TGF-β1 and SMAD2 by CST@GOA may also contribute to the enhanced bone regeneration observed by micro-CT ( Fig. 5 A).

Although there is no established signature of ‘fibrosis’ in GO analysis, we have identified several fibrosis-related DEPs based on literature that may explain the attenuation of chronic FBR by SPD-functionalized biomatrix. CST@GOA downregulates the expression of COL3A1, ACTA2 (α-SMA), fibulin 2 (FBNL2) and syndecan 3 (SDC3) ( Fig. 8 G), which are known to mediate the fibrosis caused by skeletal cells expressing leptin receptor (LEPR) [ 15 ]. The downregulation of COL3A1 and ACTA2 by CST@GOA also corroborates with the results of IF against COL3A1 and ACTA2 in the peri-implant tissues ( Fig. S21 ). Notably, the level of ACTA2 is upregulated by CDT@GOA in both our proteomic data and IF staining ( Fig. 8 G and S21 ), which indicates opposite functions of SPD and DETA again. In addition, S100 calcium-binding protein A8 (S100A8), another known mediator of fibrosis [ 89 ], is also decreased by CST@GOA.

The above bioactivities of the SPD-functionalized biomatrix may involve multiple signaling pathways. Therefore, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis was conducted to identify the most relevant pathways. Among the top 12 enriched pathways ( Fig. S27 ), PI3K-Akt signaling pathway is regarded as the main pathway that coordinates downstream signaling of inflammation, autophagy and bone homeostasis. 9, 15 and 12 DEPs in this pathway were identified for CST@GOA vs. Scaffold or C@GOA or CDT@GOA, respectively, much more than 3 DEPs of CDT@GOA vs. Scaffold ( Fig. 8 H). Surprisingly, PTEN, a negative regulator of PI3K-Akt pathway, is found to be evidently upregulated by CST@GOA vs. the other three ( Fig. 8 I). The upregulation of PTEN is known to inhibit the phosphorylation of Akt, which is known to activate downstream NF-κB signaling via the phosphorylation of IKK [ 90 , 91 ]. Hence, the upregulation of PTEN by CST@GOA should inhibit NF-κB signaling, which not only agrees with our previous results [ 45 ], but also is line with the downregulated phosphorylation of IκBα and p65 observed in vitro ( Fig. 7 F). Consistently, three important factors in the NF-κB pathway are found to be significantly downregulated by CST@GOA in our proteomic data ( Fig. 8 J), including TRAF1, protein kinase C beta (PRKCB) and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma translocation protein 1 (MALT1). Together, our results indicate that the upregulation of PTEN by CST@GOA leads to the inhibition of NF-κB signaling downstream of the PI3K-Akt pathway.

Akt is also known to inhibit autophagy by inhibiting AMPK, an inhibitor of mTOR signaling [ 92 ]. Therefore, the upregulation of PTEN by CST@GOA should enhance the activation of AMPK and thus inhibit downstream mTOR signaling, which is corroborated by our in vitro results ( Fig. 7 F). Our in vitro results of the reduced p62 level and the decreased ratio of LC3β I to LC3β II also indicated that the inhibition of mTOR activity by CST@GOA indeed induced autophagy ( Fig. 7 G). In our proteomic data, 8 upregulated proteins and 3 downregulated ones were identified in CST@GOA vs. CDT@GOA for the autophagy pathway ( Fig. 8 K). Among these hits are two key autophagy markers, GABA type A receptor-associated protein (GABARAP) and sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1 or p62). GABARAP, a positive autophagy marker, is upregulated by CST@GOA but downregulated by CDT@GOA. In contrast, SQSTM1/p62, a negative autophagy marker, is downregulated by CST@GOA but upregulated by CDT@GOA. Together, our results indicate that CST@GOA induces autophagy downstream of the PI3K-Akt pathway, which is medicated through a triple negative mechanism of Akt-inhibiting-AMPK, AMPK-inhibiting-mTOR and mTOR-inhibiting-autophagy ( Fig. 8 L). Additionally, we have also found the upregulation of DEP domain-containing mTOR-interacting protein (DEPTOR), a known inhibitor of mTOR, and the downregulation of casein kinase 1α1 (CSNK1A1), the inhibiting kinase of DEPTOR by CST@GOA ( Fig. 8 K), which also suggests an inhibition of mTOR downstream of the PI3K-Akt pathway [ 93 ].

Last but not least, the upregulation of PTEN may also contributes to bone regeneration. Bone homeostasis is a dynamic process between inflammatory response and bone generation, which relies on the coordinated activities of osteoblasts, osteoclasts and macrophages [ 94 ]. Some recent works have demonstrated that the inhibition of the PI3K-Akt pathway can promote osteogenesis through the activation of autophagy [ 95 , 96 ] or the inhibition of osteoclast differentiation [ [97] , [98] , [99] ]. So, bone homeostasis is a complicated scenario related to inflammation and autophagy downstream of the PI3K-Akt pathway. We have found that CST@GOA can promote the differentiation of macrophages toward the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype in vitro ( Fig. 7 B-E), while inhibiting osteoclast differentiation ( Fig. 7 G-J) and fostering osteoblast differentiation ( Fig. 6 ). Our in vitro data also shows the downregulation of NFATC1, an effector for osteoclast differentiation downstream of NF-κB signaling, for CST@GOA ( Fig. 7 J). Consistently, our proteomic data indicates the inhibition of inflammation and induction of autophagy by CST@GOA downstream of the PI3K-Akt pathway. In addition, several DEPs of the PI3K-Akt pathway identified in our proteomic data also imply improved bone homeostasis for CST@GOA ( Fig. 8 I). First, integrin-binding sialoprotein (IBSP), a protein that binds tightly to hydroxyapatite, is found to be upregulated in CST@GOA vs. CDT@GOA. Second, thrombospondin-3 (THBS3), a protein implicated in fibrosis formation, is upregulated by CDT@GOA, but downregulated by CST@GOA. Third, integrin alpha-IIb (ITGA2B), a receptor for fibronectin and fibrinogen, is also upregulated by CST@GOA. These findings suggest that CST@GOA may nurture osseointegration via two mechanisms downstream of the PI3K-Akt pathway: one is by overexpression of hydroxyapatite-binding proteins to form brick-and-mortar bone structure; the other is via inhibiting fibrosis and unblocking angiogenesis.

Our proteomic data has revealed various potential mechanisms for SPD-functionalized biomatrix. We have only dissected the sections related to immune responses, autophagy and bone homeostasis, as well as selected fibrosis-related proteins. It is found that most of these proteins, if not all of them, are downstream of the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway ( Fig. 8 L). Hence, it is hypothesized that the upregulation of PTEN by SPD plays a pivotal role in coordinating these downstream signaling.
sections.conclusion: In summary, we have developed composite scaffolds with interpenetrating hard and soft phases to promote bone regeneration, which consist of titanium alloy scaffolds with TPMS structure and spermidine-functionalized biomatrices (CST@GOA). More importantly, we have demonstrated that both synthetic polymer (silicone) and metal (Ti-6Al-4V) implants can be modified by CST@GOA to reduce acute inflammatory response and fibrosis caused by exogenous materials. First, our in vitro cell experiments show that CST@GOA not only inhibits inflammatory responses and osteoclastogenesis of macrophages, but also fosters migration and osteogenesis of MC3T3-E1 cells. Second, the implantation in rats verifies that CST@GOA is able to mitigate acute inflammation and fibrosis, characteristics of acute and chronic FBR, against silicone. Third, the bone regeneration experiment in rabbits demonstrates that CST@GOA-interpenetrated scaffolds can attenuate FBR against Ti-6Al-4V implants and promote osseointegration. Meanwhile, DETA, a polyamine resembling spermidine in chemistry, has been used in place of spermidine to enable ‘operando’ comparison in both cell and animal experiments. Our proteomic analysis of rabbit bone tissues suggests that spermidine modulates PI3K-Akt pathway by upregulating PTEN, which may play a central role in coordinating downstream signaling of inflammation, autophagy and bone homeostasis. Together, spermidine can empower various implants with anti -FBR activity and nurture peri-implant niche to improve osseointegration of metal implants. Given that spermidine is a simple natural molecule that exists in our bodies, it is believed that spermidine affords a safer and more elegant strategy to alleviate FBR against medical implants than conventional approaches.
